questions.prompt: How many positive factors does 48 have?
questions.explanation:
Prime-factorise: 48 = 16 × 3 = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>1</sup>.

Number of factors = (4 + 1)(1 + 1) = 5 × 2 = 10.

You can confirm by listing them in pairs: 1 & 48, 2 & 24, 3 & 16, 4 & 12, 6 & 8. That's five pairs, so ten factors.

The formula is faster and, more importantly, it doesn't let you skip one when you're tired.
questions.tip: Add 1 to every exponent in the prime factorisation, then multiply.
questions.trap: Multiplying the exponents (4 × 1 = 4) instead of adding 1 to each first. The exponent 0 is also a choice for each prime.

questions.prompt: Which of the following integers is divisible by 9?
questions.explanation:
A number is divisible by 9 exactly when its digit sum is divisible by 9.

- 4,563: 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 = 18, divisible by 9. Yes.
- 5,412: 5 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 12, no.
- 7,321: 13, no.
- 8,104: 13, no.
- 6,215: 14, no.

Only 4,563 works. Check: 4,563 ÷ 9 = 507.
questions.tip: Digit sum divisible by 9 means the number is divisible by 9.
questions.trap: 5,412 has a digit sum of 12, which is divisible by 3 but not by 9. It's the 'divisible by 3' rule used on a 9 question.

questions.prompt: What is the greatest common divisor of 24 and 36?
questions.explanation:
Prime-factorise: 24 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3 and 36 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup>.

The GCD takes each shared prime at its lower power: 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 = 12.

Check: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3, and 2 and 3 share no common factor, so nothing bigger works.
questions.tip: GCD means shared primes at the lower exponent; LCM means all primes at the higher exponent.
questions.trap: 72 is the LCM, not the GCD. Read whether the question says 'greatest common divisor' or 'least common multiple' before you start.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of all the prime numbers between 20 and 40?
questions.explanation:
List the numbers from 21 to 39 and cross out the non-primes.

- 21 = 3 × 7, 22 even, 24 even, 25 = 5 × 5, 26 even, 27 = 3 × 9, 28 even.
- 30 even, 32 even, 33 = 3 × 11, 34 even, 35 = 5 × 7, 36 even, 38 even, 39 = 3 × 13.

Primes left: 23, 29, 31, 37. Sum = 23 + 29 + 31 + 37 = 120.

You only need to test divisibility by 2, 3 and 5 here, because the next prime, 7, has a square (49) bigger than 40.
questions.tip: To test primes below 49, check divisibility by 2, 3 and 5 (and 7 only for numbers like 49).
questions.trap: Counting 21, 27, 33 or 39 as prime because they look odd and 'random'. Every one of them is a multiple of 3.

questions.prompt: Three signal lights blink every 8, 12 and 18 minutes. They all blink together at 6:00 a.m. At what time will they next blink together?
questions.explanation:
'Together again' means LCM.

8 = 2<sup>3</sup>, 12 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3, 18 = 2 × 3<sup>2</sup>. Take every prime at its highest power: 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> = 72.

They next blink together 72 minutes after 6:00, which is 7:12 a.m.

The wrong times come from using only two of the three intervals: LCM(8, 12) = 24 gives 6:24 and LCM(12, 18) = 36 gives 6:36.
questions.tip: Bells, buses and lights that repeat at fixed gaps are LCM problems.
questions.trap: Using the LCM of just two of the three intervals. The answer has to work for all three lights.

questions.prompt: How many of the positive factors of 60 are odd?
questions.explanation:
60 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 × 5.

An odd factor can't contain any 2, so use the 2 exponent 0 only. That leaves choices only for 3 (0 or 1) and 5 (0 or 1): 2 × 2 = 4 odd factors.

They are 1, 3, 5 and 15.

For comparison, the total number of factors is 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.
questions.tip: For odd factors, delete the 2s from the factorisation, then count what remains.
questions.trap: Answering 12, the total number of factors. The question only asks about the odd ones.

questions.prompt: How many trailing zeros does 30! have?
questions.explanation:
Each trailing zero needs a factor of 10 = 2 × 5. In 30! the 2s are plentiful, so count the 5s.

30 ÷ 5 = 6 (multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30).

30 ÷ 25 = 1 (the multiple 25 holds a second 5).

Total 5s: 6 + 1 = 7, so 30! ends in 7 zeros.
questions.tip: Trailing zeros in n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + ...
questions.trap: Stopping at 6 and forgetting that 25 contributes two 5s.

questions.prompt: If n is a positive integer and n² is divisible by 72, what is the smallest possible value of n?
questions.explanation:
72 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup>.

n² has every prime exponent doubled. For n² to contain at least 2<sup>3</sup>, n² needs 2<sup>4</sup> (exponents of a square are even, so round 3 up to 4). For 3<sup>2</sup>, n² needs 3<sup>2</sup>.

So n² must be a multiple of 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> = 144, which means n is a multiple of 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 = 12.

Check: 12² = 144 = 2 × 72. ✓. And 6² = 36 is not divisible by 72.
questions.tip: For 'n² is divisible by k', round every exponent in k up to even, then halve.
questions.trap: Choosing 6, the square root of 36 or the 'half-way' number. 6² = 36 is smaller than 72, so it can't be divisible by it.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive integer k such that 360k is a perfect square?
questions.explanation:
360 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5.

A perfect square has all even exponents. The 3<sup>2</sup> is fine. The 2<sup>3</sup> and 5<sup>1</sup> have odd exponents, so k must supply one more 2 and one more 5.

k = 2 × 5 = 10, and 360 × 10 = 3,600 = 60². ✓
questions.tip: To make a perfect square, multiply by every prime with an odd exponent, once each.
questions.trap: Choosing 5 or 2 alone fixes only one of the two odd exponents. Check every prime.

questions.prompt: How many positive integers less than 100 are divisible by both 4 and 6?
questions.explanation:
Divisible by both 4 and 6 means divisible by LCM(4, 6) = 12.

Multiples of 12 below 100: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96. That's 8 numbers (100 ÷ 12 is about 8.3, so there are 8 whole multiples).

The wrong answers come from counting multiples of only one of the numbers: 99 ÷ 4 gives 24 multiples of 4, and 99 ÷ 6 gives 16 multiples of 6.
questions.tip: 'Divisible by both a and b' means 'divisible by the LCM of a and b'.
questions.trap: Counting multiples of 4 (24) or multiples of 6 (16). The number must satisfy both conditions.

questions.prompt: How many positive factors of 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 are multiples of 6?
questions.explanation:
A factor that's a multiple of 6 must contain at least one 2 and at least one 3. Build the factor prime by prime.

- Power of 2: 2<sup>1</sup>, 2<sup>2</sup> or 2<sup>3</sup>, so 3 choices.
- Power of 3: 3<sup>1</sup> or 3<sup>2</sup>, so 2 choices.
- Power of 5: 5<sup>0</sup> or 5<sup>1</sup>, so 2 choices.

Total = 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

A neat alternate method: factors that are multiples of 6 are 6 times a factor of 360 ÷ 6 = 60 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 × 5. That has 3 × 2 × 2 = 12 factors.
questions.tip: For 'factors that are multiples of m', fix the required primes at their minimum power and count the remaining choices.
questions.trap: Counting from exponent 0 for every prime. That would give the total of 24 factors, not just the multiples of 6.

questions.prompt: If m = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3 × 5<sup>2</sup> and n = 2 × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5, what is the value of LCM(m, n) ÷ GCD(m, n)?
questions.explanation:
LCM takes the higher power of each prime: 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>.

GCD takes the lower power of each prime: 2 × 3 × 5.

Divide: LCM ÷ GCD = 2<sup>3−1</sup> × 3<sup>2−1</sup> × 5<sup>2−1</sup> = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3 × 5 = 60.

No multiplication to big numbers needed. (Check: LCM = 1,800, GCD = 30, and 1,800 ÷ 30 = 60.)
questions.tip: LCM ÷ GCD is just the leftover exponents, and prime-by-prime subtraction avoids big numbers.
questions.trap: Answering 30, the GCD itself. Re-read which quantity the question wants.

questions.prompt: How many of the positive factors of 1,800 are perfect squares?
questions.explanation:
1,800 = 18 × 100 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>2</sup>.

A factor is a perfect square only if every prime exponent in it is even, and each exponent can't exceed the original.

- Power of 2: 0 or 2 (not 1 or 3), so 2 choices.
- Power of 3: 0 or 2, so 2 choices.
- Power of 5: 0 or 2, so 2 choices.

Total = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. They are 1, 4, 9, 25, 36, 100, 225 and 900.
questions.tip: Perfect-square factors use only even exponents up to the original exponent.
questions.trap: Giving 36, the total number of factors, or 9, which is what you get by counting 2<sup>0</sup>, 2<sup>1</sup>, 2<sup>2</sup> ... for the 2s. The exponent 3 on the 2 is odd, so only 2<sup>0</sup> and 2<sup>2</sup> are allowed.

questions.prompt: What is the greatest integer k for which 45<sup>k</sup> is a factor of 50!?
questions.explanation:
45 = 3<sup>2</sup> × 5, so 45<sup>k</sup> = 3<sup>2k</sup> × 5<sup>k</sup>.

Count the 3s in 50!: 16 + 5 + 1 = 22. Count the 5s: 10 + 2 = 12.

From the 3s: 2k ≤ 22, so k ≤ 11. From the 5s: k ≤ 12. The tighter limit rules, so k = 11.

The 5s look like the scarce prime (12 is much less than 22), but each 45 needs two 3s and only one 5, so the 3s run out first.
questions.tip: For a composite divisor, divide each prime's count by the exponent it needs, then take the smallest result.
questions.trap: Counting only the 5s (answer 12) because 5 is usually the rarer prime. Here the 3 is squared, so check both.

questions.prompt: How many integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 have exactly 3 positive factors?
questions.explanation:
A number with exactly three factors must be the square of a prime: p<sup>2</sup> has factors 1, p, p<sup>2</sup>. (Any other factorisation gives more factors, since the count formula (a + 1)(b + 1)... equals 3 only when there's a single prime with exponent 2.)

Squares of primes up to 200: 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, 5<sup>2</sup> = 25, 7<sup>2</sup> = 49, 11<sup>2</sup> = 121, 13<sup>2</sup> = 169. Next, 17<sup>2</sup> = 289, is too big.

That's 6 numbers.
questions.tip: Exactly three factors means 'prime squared'.
questions.trap: Stopping at 49 (the squares under 100) and giving 4. The limit here is 200, so 121 and 169 count too.

questions.prompt: How many positive factors of 10<sup>4</sup> are divisible by 10?
questions.explanation:
10<sup>4</sup> = 2<sup>4</sup> × 5<sup>4</sup>.

A factor divisible by 10 needs at least one 2 and at least one 5.

- Power of 2: 1 to 4, so 4 choices.
- Power of 5: 1 to 4, so 4 choices.

Total = 4 × 4 = 16.

Alternative: factors of 10<sup>4</sup> divisible by 10 are 10 times factors of 10<sup>3</sup>. Since 10<sup>3</sup> = 2<sup>3</sup> × 5<sup>3</sup> has 4 × 4 = 16 factors, the answer is 16.
questions.tip: 'Divisible by m' lets you divide the number by m first and count the factors of what's left.
questions.trap: Answering 25, the total number of factors of 10<sup>4</sup> (5 × 5). The question only wants the ones divisible by 10.

questions.prompt: For every prime number p greater than 3, what is the greatest integer that must be a divisor of p² − 1?
questions.explanation:
Factor: p² − 1 = (p − 1)(p + 1). These are two consecutive even numbers, with p − 1, p, p + 1 being three consecutive integers.

- Because p is odd, p − 1 and p + 1 are consecutive evens, so one of them is a multiple of 4. Together they supply at least 2 × 4 = 8.
- Among three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3. It isn't p (p is prime and above 3), so it's p − 1 or p + 1. That adds a factor of 3.

So 8 × 3 = 24 always divides p² − 1.

Is 24 the greatest? Try p = 5: 24. Since 24 itself is a value, nothing bigger can always divide it. (p = 7 gives 48, p = 11 gives 120, but those don't prove 48 always works because p = 5 gives 24.)
questions.tip: Factor p² − 1 into (p − 1)(p + 1) and think 'consecutive evens' plus 'one of three consecutive is a multiple of 3'.
questions.trap: Picking 48 because p = 7 gives 48. A claim about every prime must survive the smallest case, p = 5.

questions.prompt: Two positive integers a and b have a greatest common divisor of 6 and a least common multiple of 180. How many ordered pairs (a, b) are possible?
questions.explanation:
Write a = 6x and b = 6y, where x and y have no common factor (otherwise the GCD would be bigger than 6).

Then LCM = 6xy, so 6xy = 180, giving xy = 30.

Now count the ordered pairs (x, y) with xy = 30 and gcd(x, y) = 1. Since 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, each prime goes wholly to x or wholly to y (if a prime were split, both would share it). That's 2 choices for each of 3 primes: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 ordered pairs.

They are (x, y) = (1, 30), (2, 15), (3, 10), (5, 6) and the reverses. So a, b ∈ {6 and 180, 12 and 90, 18 and 60, 30 and 36}, giving 8 ordered pairs.
questions.tip: Divide out the GCD (a = gcd × x, b = gcd × y); x and y must be coprime, and their product is LCM ÷ GCD.
questions.trap: Counting unordered pairs (4). The question asks for ordered pairs, and (6, 180) is different from (180, 6).

questions.prompt: Which of the following integers is a prime number?
questions.explanation:
Test each choice for small prime divisors.

- 51: digit sum 6, so divisible by 3 (51 = 3 × 17).
- 57: digit sum 12, divisible by 3 (57 = 3 × 19).
- 63: divisible by 3 and 7.
- 91 = 7 × 13.
- 59: not divisible by 2, 3 or 5. Try 7: 7 × 8 = 56 and 7 × 9 = 63, so no. Since 8² = 64 > 59, no more tests are needed.

So 59 is prime.
questions.tip: To test primality up to about 120, try 2, 3, 5, 7 (and 11 above 120).
questions.trap: 91 looks prime because it's odd and not a multiple of 3, 5 or 11, but 7 × 13 = 91. Always test 7.

questions.prompt: What is the least positive integer that is divisible by each of the integers from 1 through 6, inclusive?
questions.explanation:
The answer is LCM(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). Take each prime at its highest power: 2<sup>2</sup> (from 4), 3 (from 3 or 6), and 5. So LCM = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60.

Check: 60 ÷ 4 = 15, 60 ÷ 6 = 10, 60 ÷ 5 = 12. ✓

The other choices are traps. 30 isn't divisible by 4. 120 and 360 and 720 are also divisible by all six, but they're not the least.
questions.tip: Don't multiply everything (6! = 720); take each prime once at its highest power.
questions.trap: Choosing 720 (6!) or 30 (2 × 3 × 5, which forgets that 4 needs 2<sup>2</sup>).

questions.prompt: How many positive factors does 540 have?
questions.explanation:
Factorise: 540 = 54 × 10 = (2 × 3<sup>3</sup>) × (2 × 5) = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>3</sup> × 5.

Number of factors = (2 + 1)(3 + 1)(1 + 1) = 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.

The common slip is mis-factorising 54 as 2 × 3<sup>2</sup> × ... Do a quick re-multiplication: 4 × 27 × 5 = 540. ✓
questions.tip: Always multiply the prime powers back to confirm the factorisation before counting.
questions.trap: Mis-reading 54 = 2 × 3<sup>3</sup> as 2 × 3<sup>2</sup>, which gives 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 factors.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest integer greater than 200 that is divisible by both 18 and 24?
questions.explanation:
Divisible by both means divisible by LCM(18, 24). 18 = 2 × 3<sup>2</sup>, 24 = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3, so LCM = 2<sup>3</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> = 72.

Multiples of 72: 72, 144, 216, ... The first one above 200 is 216.

Check: 216 ÷ 18 = 12 and 216 ÷ 24 = 9. ✓

240 is divisible by 24 but not by 18; 252 by 18 but not by 24.
questions.tip: Find the LCM first, then list its multiples near the target.
questions.trap: Choosing 240 (multiple of 24 only) or 252 (multiple of 18 only). Test both conditions.

questions.prompt: How many positive factors of 180 are NOT multiples of 3?
questions.explanation:
180 = 2<sup>2</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5.

A factor that isn't a multiple of 3 contains no 3 at all, so the exponent of 3 is 0. That leaves choices only for 2 (0, 1 or 2: three choices) and 5 (0 or 1: two choices): 3 × 2 = 6.

They are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 20.

Sanity check: total factors = 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. Multiples of 3 = 3 × 2 × 2 = 12. And 18 − 12 = 6. ✓
questions.tip: 'Not a multiple of p' means exponent of p is 0; count what's left.
questions.trap: Answering 12, the number of factors that ARE multiples of 3, or 18 (all of them).

questions.prompt: What is the smallest odd positive integer with exactly 6 positive factors?
questions.explanation:
Six factors means the exponents satisfy (a + 1)(b + 1)... = 6. The only ways: one prime to the 5th power (a = 5), or one prime squared times another prime (a = 2, b = 1).

For an odd number we use odd primes.

- Fifth power: 3<sup>5</sup> = 243.
- p<sup>2</sup> × q: 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 = 45, 5<sup>2</sup> × 3 = 75, 3<sup>2</sup> × 7 = 63.

The smallest is 45. Quick check of the nearby choices: 27 = 3<sup>3</sup> has only 4 factors and 81 = 3<sup>4</sup> has 5.
questions.tip: Break the target factor count into a product to list the possible prime-exponent patterns, then try the smallest primes.
questions.trap: Choosing 27 or 81 because small prime powers feel 'small'. Count their factors before accepting them.

questions.prompt: For how many positive integers n does n! have exactly 5 trailing zeros?
questions.explanation:
Trailing zeros in n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ...

Track the count as n grows:

- 20!, 21!, 22!, 23!, 24!: each has 4 zeros.
- 25!: n ÷ 5 = 5 and n ÷ 25 = 1, so 6 zeros.

The count jumps from 4 straight to 6 at n = 25, because 25 holds two factors of 5. So no factorial has exactly 5 trailing zeros.

The answer is 0.
questions.tip: The zero count can skip values at multiples of 25, 125 and so on.
questions.trap: Answering 5 because 'each block of five consecutive n shares a count'. That pattern holds below 25 but fails at 25.

questions.prompt: How many positive factors of 12<sup>6</sup> are multiples of 12<sup>2</sup>?
questions.explanation:
12<sup>6</sup> = (2<sup>2</sup> × 3)<sup>6</sup> = 2<sup>12</sup> × 3<sup>6</sup>, and 12<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>4</sup> × 3<sup>2</sup>.

A factor that is a multiple of 12<sup>2</sup> has a power of 2 from 4 to 12 (9 choices) and a power of 3 from 2 to 6 (5 choices).

Total = 9 × 5 = 45.

Cross-check: these factors are 12<sup>2</sup> times a factor of 12<sup>4</sup> = 2<sup>8</sup> × 3<sup>4</sup>, which has 9 × 5 = 45 factors. ✓
questions.tip: Count the choices from 'required minimum' up to 'available maximum' for each prime.
questions.trap: Answering 91, the total number of factors of 12<sup>6</sup> (13 × 7). Or counting 12 − 4 = 8 choices instead of 9; the range 4 to 12 includes both ends.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by 6, is not divisible by 4, and has exactly 12 positive factors?
questions.explanation:
The number is divisible by 6 but not by 4, so it has exactly one factor of 2 and at least one 3. Write n = 2 × m, where m is odd and divisible by 3.

Factor count: 2 × (factors of m) = 12, so m has exactly 6 factors. Odd numbers with 6 factors are p<sup>2</sup> × q or p<sup>5</sup>. With 3 required: 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 = 45, 5<sup>2</sup> × 3 = 75, 3<sup>2</sup> × 7 = 63, 3<sup>5</sup> = 243.

Smallest m = 45, so n = 90.

Check: 90 = 2 × 3<sup>2</sup> × 5 has (1 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 12 factors, is divisible by 6, and 90 ÷ 4 isn't an integer.

The other choices all have 12 factors but are divisible by 4.
questions.tip: Translate every condition into prime exponents (here: 2<sup>1</sup> exactly) before hunting for numbers.
questions.trap: 60, 72, 84 and 108 each have 12 factors and are divisible by 6, but they all contain 2<sup>2</sup>, which breaks 'not divisible by 4'.

questions.prompt: The sum of two positive integers a and b is 100, and their greatest common divisor is 20. How many ordered pairs (a, b) are possible?
questions.explanation:
Since the GCD is 20, write a = 20x and b = 20y, where x and y share no common factor.

Then a + b = 20(x + y) = 100, so x + y = 5.

Positive integer pairs adding to 5: (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1). Each pair has no common factor (5 is prime, so x and y can't both share one). So all four work.

The pairs (a, b) are (20, 80), (40, 60), (60, 40), (80, 20). The answer is 4.

Check: GCD(40, 60) = 20 ✓ and GCD(20, 80) = 20 ✓.
questions.tip: With 'GCD = g', set a = gx and b = gy with gcd(x, y) = 1, then solve in x and y.
questions.trap: Answering 2 by counting unordered pairs, or 3/6 by testing a few values and giving up.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 58 is divided by 7?
questions.explanation:
Find the largest multiple of 7 that fits into 58: 7 × 8 = 56.

Then 58 = 7 × 8 + 2, so the quotient is 8 and the remainder is 2.

A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor, so the answer has to be one of 0 to 6. That fact also helps you eliminate junk choices quickly.
questions.tip: Find the biggest multiple of the divisor that doesn't exceed the number; the leftover is the remainder.
questions.trap: Giving the quotient (8) instead of the remainder, or stopping at a multiple like 7 × 7 = 49 and writing 9, which is bigger than the divisor.

questions.prompt: When the positive integer n is divided by 7, the remainder is 3. What is the remainder when 4n is divided by 7?
questions.explanation:
Pick a number that fits: n = 3 (3 ÷ 7 leaves remainder 3).

Then 4n = 12, and 12 = 7 × 1 + 5, so the remainder is 5.

Check with another valid n, say n = 10: 4n = 40 = 7 × 5 + 5. Same remainder, 5.

The rule behind it: the remainder of a product equals the remainder of (4 × 3) = 12, reduced again.
questions.tip: With a remainder statement, pick the smallest number that fits and compute directly.
questions.trap: Answering 12 (4 × 3). A product of remainders can exceed the divisor, so reduce it again.

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 3<sup>10</sup>?
questions.explanation:
Units digits of powers of 3 cycle every 4: 3, 9, 7, 1, then repeat.

Divide the exponent by 4: 10 = 4 × 2 + 2, so the remainder is 2. That means the second spot in the cycle, which is 9.

Check: 3<sup>10</sup> = 59,049, which ends in 9. ✓
questions.tip: Divide the exponent by the cycle length and read the position from the remainder.
questions.trap: Using the exponent itself as a position, or using 3<sup>10</sup> ≈ 3 × 10 = 30. Always reduce the exponent first.

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 7<sup>23</sup>?
questions.explanation:
The units digits of powers of 7 cycle: 7, 9, 3, 1 (length 4).

23 = 4 × 5 + 3, so the remainder is 3 and we take the third spot in the cycle: 3.

So 7<sup>23</sup> ends in 3.

A quick way to double-check: 7<sup>20</sup> ends in 1 (five full cycles), and 7<sup>3</sup> = 343 ends in 3. 1 × 3 = 3. ✓
questions.tip: Break the exponent into 'full cycles' (which end in the cycle's last digit) plus the leftover.
questions.trap: Taking the remainder 3 and answering 1 (the end of cycle) or 7 (the start of cycle). Count carefully: remainder 3 means third spot.

questions.prompt: When a positive integer n is divided by 12, the remainder is 7. What is the remainder when n is divided by 4?
questions.explanation:
Write n = 12q + 7. Since 12q is a multiple of 4, only the 7 matters when you divide by 4. And 7 = 4 × 1 + 3, so the remainder is 3.

Pick-numbers check: n = 7 gives remainder 3 when divided by 4. n = 19 gives 19 = 4 × 4 + 3, also 3. ✓

This works because 4 is a factor of 12, so the remainders line up.
questions.tip: If the new divisor is a factor of the old one, just reduce the old remainder by the new divisor.
questions.trap: Answering 7 (the original remainder, which can't be a remainder mod 4) or 1 by guessing.

questions.prompt: Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 150 days from today?
questions.explanation:
Days of the week repeat every 7 days, so only the remainder of 150 ÷ 7 matters.

150 = 7 × 21 + 3, so the remainder is 3.

Count three days forward from Wednesday: Thursday, Friday, Saturday.

The answer is Saturday.
questions.tip: Calendar questions are 'divide by 7 and use the remainder'.
questions.trap: Counting 150 ÷ 7 ≈ 21 weeks and answering Wednesday (or Thursday). The leftover 3 days are the whole answer.

questions.prompt: If x and y are positive integers and x/y = 8.4, which of the following could be the remainder when x is divided by y?
questions.explanation:
x/y = 8.4 means x = 8y + r, so r/y = 0.4 = 2/5. Therefore r = 2y/5.

For r to be a whole number, y must be a multiple of 5. Write y = 5k; then r = 2k.

So every possible remainder is even (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, ...). Of the choices, only 10 is even: y = 25 gives r = 10, and x = 8 × 25 + 10 = 210. Check: 210 ÷ 25 = 8.4. ✓
questions.tip: Turn the decimal part into a fraction: remainder ÷ divisor = decimal part.
questions.trap: Choosing 4 (the digit after the decimal point). The remainder is 0.4 times the divisor, not 0.4 times 10.

questions.prompt: The positive integer n leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3, a remainder of 2 when divided by 4, and a remainder of 3 when divided by 5. What is the smallest possible value of n?
questions.explanation:
Look for the pattern: each remainder is exactly 2 less than its divisor (3 − 2 = 1, 4 − 2 = 2, 5 − 2 = 3). So n + 2 is divisible by 3, 4 and 5.

The smallest positive multiple of LCM(3, 4, 5) = 60 gives n + 2 = 60, so n = 58.

Check: 58 = 3 × 19 + 1 ✓, 58 = 4 × 14 + 2 ✓, 58 = 5 × 11 + 3 ✓.

If you list instead, you'd test 3, 6, ... for a long time. Spotting 'divisor minus 2' is the shortcut.
questions.tip: If the gap 'divisor − remainder' is the same every time, n + gap is a common multiple of the divisors.
questions.trap: Choosing 118, the second solution, or testing only two of the three conditions (28 works for 3 and 5 but not 4).

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 2<sup>21</sup> × 3<sup>17</sup> × 7<sup>10</sup>?
questions.explanation:
Find each units digit with its cycle, then multiply the units digits.

- 2<sup>21</sup>: cycle 2, 4, 8, 6. 21 = 4 × 5 + 1, so position 1: 2.
- 3<sup>17</sup>: cycle 3, 9, 7, 1. 17 = 4 × 4 + 1, so position 1: 3.
- 7<sup>10</sup>: cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. 10 = 4 × 2 + 2, so position 2: 9.

Product of units digits: 2 × 3 × 9 = 54, so the units digit is 4.
questions.tip: The units digit of a product depends only on the units digits of the factors.
questions.trap: Forgetting to reduce 54 to its last digit, or reading the 7<sup>10</sup> position wrongly (answer 9 is just 7<sup>10</sup>'s own digit).

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 2<sup>50</sup> is divided by 7?
questions.explanation:
Look at small powers of 2 and their remainders when divided by 7:

2<sup>1</sup> = 2, 2<sup>2</sup> = 4, 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 → remainder 1, then 2<sup>4</sup> → 2, and the pattern repeats: 2, 4, 1 (cycle length 3).

50 = 3 × 16 + 2, so the remainder is the 2nd spot in the cycle: 4.

Shortcut: 2<sup>3</sup> leaves 1, so 2<sup>48</sup> = (2<sup>3</sup>)<sup>16</sup> leaves 1. Then 2<sup>50</sup> = 2<sup>48</sup> × 2<sup>2</sup> leaves 1 × 4 = 4.
questions.tip: Find the first power that leaves remainder 1, then chop the exponent into chunks of that size.
questions.trap: Assuming the cycle is 4 long (as for units digits). For divisor 7 the cycle is 3. Always find the cycle for the actual divisor.

questions.prompt: When the positive integer n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when n² + n is divided by 6?
questions.explanation:
Pick n = 4. Then n² + n = 16 + 4 = 20, and 20 = 6 × 3 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

Check with n = 10: 100 + 10 = 110 = 6 × 18 + 2. Same.

Algebra confirms it: n = 6k + 4, so n² + n = 36k² + 48k + 16 + 6k + 4 = 6(...) + 20, and 20 leaves remainder 2.
questions.tip: Reduce each piece with remainders: n ≡ 4, so n² + n ≡ 16 + 4 = 20 ≡ 2.
questions.trap: Answering 20 (the unreduced value) or 4 (assuming the remainder stays the same).

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + ... + 10! is divided by 12?
questions.explanation:
For every n ≥ 4, n! contains 4 × 3 = 12 as a factor (since 4! = 24 is a multiple of 12). So 4!, 5!, ..., 10! all leave remainder 0.

Only the first three terms matter: 1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9.

9 is less than 12, so the remainder is 9.
questions.tip: In a factorial sum, find where the factorial becomes a multiple of the divisor; every later term vanishes.
questions.trap: Adding all ten factorials and drowning in big numbers. The terms from 4! onward disappear.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 7<sup>99</sup> + 9<sup>99</sup> is divided by 8?
questions.explanation:
Reduce each base modulo 8. 7 is one less than 8, so 7 behaves like −1: 7<sup>99</sup> is like (−1)<sup>99</sup> = −1, which is remainder 7. And 9 leaves remainder 1, so 9<sup>99</sup> leaves remainder 1<sup>99</sup> = 1.

Sum of remainders: 7 + 1 = 8, which is a multiple of 8, so the remainder is 0.

Check small cases: 7 + 9 = 16 (remainder 0) and 7<sup>3</sup> + 9<sup>3</sup> = 343 + 729 = 1,072 = 8 × 134. ✓
questions.tip: A base that is one below the divisor behaves like −1: odd powers give remainder (divisor − 1), even powers give 1.
questions.trap: Answering 8 (the sum of remainders) without reducing, or 1 by treating 7<sup>99</sup> as leaving remainder 1.

questions.prompt: The positive integer n leaves a remainder of 7 when divided by 12. Which of the following could be the remainder when n is divided by 8?
questions.explanation:
Write n = 12k + 7 and list a few values: 7, 19, 31, 43, 55, ...

Remainders when divided by 8: 7, 3, 7, 3, 7, ... The remainder alternates between 7 and 3.

Why? Going from one n to the next adds 12, which is 4 more than a multiple of 8, so the remainder flips between 7 and 7 + 4 − 8 = 3.

Only 3 appears among the choices.

So the remainder isn't fixed here, because 8 is not a factor of 12. 'Could be' is the clue.
questions.tip: When the new divisor isn't a factor of the old one, list several values of n to see all the possible remainders.
questions.trap: Assuming the remainder is fixed and reducing 7 by 8 in one step. That only works when the new divisor divides the old one.

questions.prompt: The positive integer p leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 6. Which of the following could be the remainder when p is divided by 9?
questions.explanation:
p = 6k + 4. List p: 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, 34, 40, ...

Remainders when divided by 9: 4, 1, 7, 4, 1, 7, ... The remainders repeat 4, 1, 7.

Only 7 is among the choices.

Reason: p is 4 more than a multiple of 6, so p ≡ 1 mod 3. Remainders when divided by 9 must also leave 1 when divided by 3. Among 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, only 7 fits (7 = 3 × 2 + 1). ✓
questions.tip: If the divisors share a factor (here 3), remainders must stay consistent with that factor.
questions.trap: Testing one value of p and choosing its remainder. Check enough values to see the full pattern, or use the shared-factor argument.

questions.prompt: In a year that is not a leap year, January 1 falls on a Friday. On what day of the week does November 1 of the same year fall?
questions.explanation:
Count the days from January 1 to November 1. The months January through October have 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 304 days.

304 = 7 × 43 + 3, so the remainder is 3. Move forward 3 days from Friday: Saturday, Sunday, Monday.

November 1 is a Monday.
questions.tip: Add up the days between the two dates, divide by 7, and step forward by the remainder.
questions.trap: Using 31 days for every month, or including February as 29 days. The problem says it's not a leap year.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 2<sup>100</sup> + 3<sup>100</sup> is divided by 15?
questions.explanation:
Work with each term separately.

2<sup>100</sup>: 2<sup>4</sup> = 16 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 15. So 2<sup>100</sup> = (2<sup>4</sup>)<sup>25</sup> leaves 1<sup>25</sup> = 1.

3<sup>100</sup>: 3 shares a factor with 15, so it never returns to 1. Remainders of 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, ... divided by 15: 3, 9, 12, 6, 3, 9, 12, 6, ... a cycle of length 4. 100 = 4 × 25, so we're at the 4th spot: 6.

Sum: 1 + 6 = 7, which is under 15, so the remainder is 7.
questions.tip: A cycle that returns to 1 only exists when the base and divisor share no factor; otherwise list the remainders and look for the repeat.
questions.trap: Assuming 3<sup>100</sup> leaves remainder 1 like 2<sup>100</sup> does (giving 2), or reading position 4 as 3.

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 7<sup>(7<sup>7</sup>)</sup>?
questions.explanation:
The tower means 7 raised to the power (7<sup>7</sup>), not (7<sup>7</sup>)<sup>7</sup>. The exponent is the huge number 7<sup>7</sup> = 823,543.

Units digits of powers of 7 repeat every 4, so we need the exponent 7<sup>7</sup> modulo 4. Since 7 leaves remainder 3 (or −1) when divided by 4, and the power is odd, 7<sup>7</sup> leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4. (Check: 823,543 = 4 × 205,885 + 3.)

The 3rd spot in the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 is 3.

So the units digit is 3.
questions.tip: For a power tower, reduce the top exponent modulo the cycle length first (4 for units digits of 2, 3, 7, 8).
questions.trap: Reducing the exponent as 7 mod 4 = 3 is right, but some people then use 7<sup>3</sup>'s position wrongly, or think 7<sup>7</sup> is 'just 7'. Evaluate the exponent's remainder carefully.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 125 is divided by 9?
questions.explanation:
9 × 13 = 117, and 9 × 14 = 126 is too big. So 125 = 9 × 13 + 8.

The remainder is 8.

Quick check using digit sums: the digit sum of 125 is 8, and since 9 divides 99 and 9, the remainder when divided by 9 equals the digit sum (reduced). That agrees.
questions.tip: For divisor 9, the remainder equals the digit sum, reduced until it's below 9.
questions.trap: Giving the quotient 13, or 9 (a remainder can't equal the divisor).

questions.prompt: When the positive integer n is divided by 11, the remainder is 6. What is the remainder when 3n is divided by 11?
questions.explanation:
Pick n = 6 (6 ÷ 11 leaves remainder 6). Then 3n = 18, and 18 = 11 × 1 + 7.

The remainder is 7.

Check with n = 17: 3n = 51 = 11 × 4 + 7. ✓
questions.tip: Multiply the remainder by the multiplier, then reduce again.
questions.trap: Answering 18 without reducing, or 6 by assuming the remainder stays the same after multiplying.

questions.prompt: Today is a Monday. What day of the week will it be 1,000 days from today?
questions.explanation:
Only the remainder when dividing by 7 matters. 1,000 = 7 × 142 + 6 (since 7 × 142 = 994).

Six days after Monday: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

The answer is Sunday.

A nice shortcut: 6 days forward is one day back, and one day before Monday is Sunday.
questions.tip: Moving forward by remainder 6 is the same as moving back 1 day.
questions.trap: Using 1,000 ÷ 7 ≈ 143 and miscounting the leftover, or answering Monday (a multiple of 7 days).

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 8<sup>42</sup> − 6<sup>40</sup>?
questions.explanation:
8<sup>42</sup>: units digits of powers of 8 cycle 8, 4, 2, 6. 42 = 4 × 10 + 2, so position 2: 4.

6<sup>40</sup>: every power of 6 ends in 6.

Subtract: ...4 − ...6. Borrow from the tens place: 14 − 6 = 8. The number 8<sup>42</sup> is far larger than 6<sup>40</sup>, so the difference is positive and the units digit is 8.

A common slip is computing 4 − 6 = −2 and writing 2 as the units digit.
questions.tip: When the first units digit is smaller, borrow 10 (so 4 − 6 becomes 14 − 6 = 8).
questions.trap: Answering 2 from 6 − 4 or from the negative −2. The units digit of a positive number is never negative.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest positive integer that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 4, by 6 and by 10, and is also divisible by 7?
questions.explanation:
Leaving remainder 1 for divisors 4, 6 and 10 means n − 1 is a multiple of LCM(4, 6, 10) = 60. So n = 60k + 1: 61, 121, 181, 241, 301, 361, ...

Now test divisibility by 7:

- 61, 121, 181, 241: not multiples of 7 (7 × 8 = 56, 7 × 17 = 119, 7 × 25 = 175, 7 × 34 = 238).
- 301 = 7 × 43. ✓

So the smallest is 301.

The choices 61, 121, 361 and 421 all satisfy the remainder conditions but are not divisible by 7.
questions.tip: Build the family n = LCM × k + r, then step through it until the extra condition holds.
questions.trap: Answering 61, which meets the remainder conditions but ignores 'divisible by 7'.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 3<sup>40</sup> is divided by 7?
questions.explanation:
Find the cycle of 3<sup>k</sup> mod 7:

3, 9 → 2, 6, 18 → 4, 12 → 5, 15 → 1. So the remainders are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 and then repeat: the cycle length is 6.

40 = 6 × 6 + 4, so we take the 4th spot: 4.

Shortcut: 3<sup>6</sup> leaves remainder 1 when divided by 7, so 3<sup>36</sup> leaves 1 and 3<sup>40</sup> leaves the same remainder as 3<sup>4</sup> = 81 = 7 × 11 + 4.
questions.tip: Don't assume a cycle length of 4; compute the remainders until you hit 1 again.
questions.trap: Using the units-digit cycle length 4 (40 ÷ 4 leaves 0, last position) and picking 5 or 1. This is a divisor-7 problem, and its cycle is 6.

questions.prompt: x and y are positive integers with x/y = 5.35 and y < 50. What is the greatest possible remainder when x is divided by y?
questions.explanation:
x = 5y + r, so r/y = 0.35 = 7/20. Then r = 7y/20, which means y must be a multiple of 20.

With y < 50, the options are y = 20 (r = 7) and y = 40 (r = 14). The next, y = 60, is too big.

Greatest possible remainder: 14.

Check: y = 40, r = 14 gives x = 5 × 40 + 14 = 214, and 214 ÷ 40 = 5.35. ✓
questions.tip: Reduce the decimal to a fraction in lowest terms to see which divisors y are possible.
questions.trap: Answering 7 by stopping at the smallest y. The question asks for the greatest remainder.

questions.prompt: The positive integer n leaves a remainder of 5 when divided by 9 and a remainder of 7 when divided by 11. What is the smallest possible value of n?
questions.explanation:
Look at the gaps: 9 − 5 = 4 and 11 − 7 = 4. They're the same. So n + 4 is divisible by both 9 and 11. Since 9 and 11 share no factor, n + 4 is a multiple of 99, and the smallest positive n has n + 4 = 99, so n = 95.

Check: 95 = 9 × 10 + 5 ✓ and 95 = 11 × 8 + 7 ✓.

The distractors each satisfy only one condition (41 and 5 mod 9; 62 and 84 and 7 mod 11), and 194 = 95 + 99 satisfies both but isn't the smallest.
questions.tip: Check whether 'divisor − remainder' matches across the conditions; if so, n + gap is a common multiple.
questions.trap: Picking 194 (a valid but larger n) or a number that satisfies only one of the two conditions.

questions.prompt: If p and q are distinct prime numbers greater than 3, what is the remainder when p² − q² is divided by 24?
questions.explanation:
Show that p² leaves remainder 1 when divided by 24 for any prime p > 3.

p² − 1 = (p − 1)(p + 1). Since p is odd, p − 1 and p + 1 are consecutive even numbers, so one is a multiple of 4 and the product has at least 2 × 4 = 8 as a factor. Since p isn't a multiple of 3, one of p − 1 and p + 1 is, adding a factor of 3. So 24 divides p² − 1.

Hence p² ≡ 1 and q² ≡ 1 (mod 24), and p² − q² ≡ 1 − 1 = 0.

Check: p = 5, q = 7 gives 25 − 49 = −24, a multiple of 24. And p = 11, q = 5 gives 121 − 25 = 96 = 4 × 24. ✓
questions.tip: Squares of primes above 3 all leave remainder 1 when divided by 24.
questions.trap: Testing one pair and answering with its remainder. Here every pair gives 0, so the structure is the key.

questions.prompt: What is the units digit of 8<sup>(9<sup>9</sup>)</sup> + 3<sup>(4<sup>5</sup>)</sup>?
questions.explanation:
Handle each tower by reducing its exponent modulo 4 (the units-digit cycle length for 8 and 3).

First term: 9<sup>9</sup>. Since 9 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 4, 9<sup>9</sup> leaves 1<sup>9</sup> = 1. Position 1 in the cycle for 8 (8, 4, 2, 6) is 8.

Second term: 4<sup>5</sup> = 1,024, which is a multiple of 4 (remainder 0). That's the last spot of the cycle for 3 (3, 9, 7, 1): 1.

Sum of units digits: 8 + 1 = 9.
questions.tip: For towers, reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length, and treat remainder 0 as the last position.
questions.trap: Treating remainder 0 as 'the first digit of the cycle' (3 instead of 1) for the second tower, giving 8 + 3 = 11 and a units digit of 1.
